title: Statement on Inclusive and Sustainable Artificial Intelligence for People and the Planet
original_title: Déclaration sur une intelligence artificielle inclusive et durable pour les peuples et la planète
issuing_body: Signatories of the AI Action Summit, Paris (hosted by the French Presidency): 63 countries, the African Union Commission and the EU
summary: Statement of the AI Action Summit in Paris that sets six priorities: accessible AI to reduce digital divides; AI that is open, inclusive, transparent, ethical, safe, secure and trustworthy; innovation without market concentration; AI that shapes work and labour markets positively; sustainable AI; and international cooperation on governance. It commends the Bletchley and Seoul summits' work on AI safety and notes the voluntary commitments made there, says the signatories will keep addressing AI risks to information integrity and continue work on AI transparency, and reaffirms the commitment to a UN Global Dialogue on AI governance and an Independent International Scientific Panel on AI.
safety_topics: international cooperation; transparency & labelling
notes: Published on 11 February 2025, the second day of the AI Action Summit, held in Paris on 10 and 11 February 2025. The signatory list names 63 countries, the African Union Commission and the EU; the United States and the United Kingdom are not on it. A footnote limits the statement to civil applications and use of AI. Founding members launched a Public Interest AI Platform and Incubator under it. The International AI Safety Report 2025 (INT-09) was published ahead of the summit.

title: AI Impact Summit Declaration
issuing_body: Participants of the India AI Impact Summit 2026, New Delhi (hosted by the Government of India)
summary: Declaration of the AI Impact Summit in New Delhi, held after the Bletchley, Seoul and Paris summits. It calls for international cooperation along seven pillars: human capital, access for social empowerment, trustworthiness of AI systems, energy efficiency, AI in science, democratising AI resources, and AI for economic growth and social good. Its secure and trusted AI section calls secure, trustworthy and robust AI foundational to trust and recognises security in AI systems, industry-led voluntary measures, technical solutions and policy frameworks across the AI lifecycle. It notes the voluntary Trusted AI Commons, a platform of technical resources, tools, benchmarks and best practices.
safety_topics: international cooperation; evaluation & testing
notes: The declaration is headed 'AI Impact Summit Declaration, New Delhi (February 18 - 19, 2026)', and its preamble says the participants gathered in New Delhi on 19 February 2026; the European Commission announced on 20 February 2026 that the EU would endorse it, and the Australian government gives the summit as 19 and 20 February 2026, so only the month is given. The endorsement list published with the text names 89 endorsers: 87 countries, among them the USA, China, India, Russia and the UK, plus the EU and IFAD. Under its pillars the declaration takes note of voluntary deliverables, among them the Charter for the Democratic Diffusion of AI, the Global AI Impact Commons, the Trusted AI Commons and its guidance note, the International Network of AI for Science Institutions and the Voluntary Guiding Principles on Resilient, Innovative, and Efficient Artificial Intelligence.

title: The Bletchley Declaration by Countries Attending the AI Safety Summit, 1-2 November 2023
issuing_body: Governments attending the AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park (28 countries and the EU), hosted by the UK Government
summary: Declaration by 28 countries and the EU on the risks of 'frontier' AI: highly capable general-purpose models, and narrow AI with harmful capabilities, that match or exceed today's most advanced models. It warns of substantial risks from intentional misuse or unintended issues of control, names cybersecurity, biotechnology and disinformation, and sees potential for serious, even catastrophic, harm. Its agenda is a shared scientific understanding of these risks and risk-based national policies, with safety testing, evaluations and transparency from developers of frontier AI, and an international network of scientific research on frontier AI safety.
safety_topics: general-purpose / frontier AI; catastrophic risk; evaluation & testing; transparency & labelling; international cooperation; research priorities
notes: Agreed at the AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park, 1-2 November 2023; the countries represented include the US, China and the EU. New Zealand joined the commitment on 23 October 2024, and GOV.UK updated the publication on 13 February 2025 to include it as a signatory. The participants said they would meet again in 2024. The International AI Safety Report (interim report INT-08, full report INT-09) was launched at this summit. GOV.UK also offers a Latin American Spanish version of the publication.

title: Seoul Declaration for safe, innovative and inclusive AI by participants attending the Leaders' Session: AI Seoul Summit, 21 May 2024
issuing_body: Leaders of Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Republic of Korea, Singapore, UK, US and the EU (AI Seoul Summit, co-hosted by the Republic of Korea and the UK)

They support creating or expanding AI safety institutes, research programmes and supervisory bodies and networks between them, welcome the annexed Seoul Statement of Intent on AI safety science, recognise the particular responsibility of organisations developing frontier AI, note the Frontier AI Safety Commitments and back the operationalisation of the Hiroshima Process Code of Conduct.

title: Seoul Statement of Intent toward International Cooperation on AI Safety Science, AI Seoul Summit 2024 (Annex)
short_title: Seoul Statement of Intent on AI Safety Science
issuing_body: Leaders of Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Republic of Korea, Singapore, UK, US and the EU
summary: Leaders of ten countries and the EU affirm international coordination, based on openness, transparency and reciprocity, to advance the science of AI safety, and commend the creation or expansion of publicly backed institutions such as AI Safety Institutes. They intend to foster common scientific understanding, including through assessments such as the International AI Safety Report. Possible steps include sharing information about models' capabilities, limitations and risks, monitoring AI harms and safety incidents, exchanging or jointly creating evaluations and data sets, and shared technical resources. They aim to develop an international network to accelerate AI safety science.

title: Frontier AI Safety Commitments, AI Seoul Summit 2024
issuing_body: AI organisations that agreed to the commitments (20 by February 2025), announced by the UK and Republic of Korea governments at the AI Seoul Summit; published by the UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
summary: Leading AI developers commit to assess frontier-model risks across the lifecycle and to set and monitor thresholds for intolerable severe risks. They agree not to develop or deploy a model if those risks cannot be kept below the thresholds, and to maintain internal accountability. They also commit to publish a safety framework and report publicly on implementation, with deeper information shared with trusted actors such as home governments.
safety_topics: general-purpose / frontier AI; catastrophic risk; evaluation & testing; transparency & labelling; accountability & liability
notes: The UK and Republic of Korea governments announced the first 16 signatories: Amazon, Anthropic, Cohere, Google, G42, IBM, Inflection AI, Meta, Microsoft, Mistral AI, Naver, OpenAI, Samsung Electronics, Technology Innovation Institute, xAI and Zhipu.ai. Magic, Minimax, 01.ai and NVIDIA were added on 7 February 2025, making 20. Signatories undertook to publish a safety framework focused on severe risks by the next AI summit, in France (the AI Action Summit, INT-01), and to provide public updates if their approaches to the three outcomes change.

title: Seoul Ministerial Statement for advancing AI safety, innovation and inclusivity: AI Seoul Summit 2024
issuing_body: Ministers of 27 countries and a representative of the EU (AI Seoul Summit ministerial session)
summary: Ministers of 27 countries and the EU recognise their role in establishing frameworks to manage risks from frontier AI models, in promoting credible external evaluations, and in identifying, with the private sector, civil society and academia, thresholds at which unmitigated risks would be severe. Their examples are capabilities that meaningfully assist non-state actors with chemical or biological weapons, and capabilities or propensities to evade human oversight through manipulation, deception or autonomous replication. Through their AI safety institutes they plan to share best practices and evaluation datasets and to collaborate on safety testing guidelines.
safety_topics: general-purpose / frontier AI; catastrophic risk; evaluation & testing; human oversight; safety institute; international cooperation
notes: Agreed at the Ministers' Session of the AI Seoul Summit on 22 May 2024; the Republic of Korea and the United Kingdom were the summit's co-chairs. Signatories include the US, UK, India, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Türkiye, Kenya, Nigeria, Rwanda and the EU; China is not on the list. Ministers planned to develop proposals on thresholds and capabilities for consideration before the AI Action Summit in France (INT-01), and looked forward to the final International Scientific Report on the Safety of Advanced AI, whose interim report (INT-08) they noted.

title: ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics
issuing_body: ASEAN Digital Ministers (ADGMIN); published by the ASEAN Secretariat
summary: A voluntary, ASEAN-endorsed guide for organisations that design, develop and deploy traditional AI in commercial and non-military or dual-use applications, aimed at alignment and interoperability across ASEAN. It sets seven guiding principles, including transparency and explainability, security and safety, human-centricity and accountability, and a governance framework: internal governance structures, risk impact assessments that set the level of human involvement (human-in-the-loop, over-the-loop or out-of-the-loop), operations management, and disclosure of AI use to stakeholders. It recommends national and regional measures, including an ASEAN Working Group on AI Governance.

Annex A gives an AI risk impact assessment template and Annex B six use cases. Supplemented by the Expanded ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics – Generative AI (ASEAN-02), a separate publication rather than a new version of this guide.

title: Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy
issuing_body: African Union Executive Council (45th Ordinary Session, Accra); African Union Commission
summary: A development-focused continental AI strategy with a focus area on minimising AI risks. It names bias and discrimination, disinformation and manipulation of political systems, surveillance, deepfakes, cyber threats and military uses, and calls for technical standards on the safety and security of AI systems. It recommends agile, risk-based regulation, AI governance bodies and independent oversight institutions in member states, a regional AI Ethics Board to review novel large-scale AI systems, impact assessments, transparency registers, red-teaming, a centre of excellence on AI safety and security and an annual AI safety and security conference.
safety_topics: risk-based classification; deepfakes & synthetic media; national security & military; evaluation & testing; accountability & liability; international cooperation
notes: Adopted by the AU Executive Council at its 45th Ordinary Session in Accra, Ghana, on 18-19 July 2024; the AU document page is dated 9 August 2024. The foreword and executive summary speak of five focus areas and fifteen action areas, while section 2.4 lists six focus areas, the sixth being an inclusive governance and regulatory framework. Implementation is planned for 2025-2030: a first phase in 2025-2026, a mid-term review in 2027 and a second phase from 2028. The AU publishes the strategy in English, French, Arabic and Portuguese.
scope_note: Mainly a development strategy for harnessing AI's benefits, building capabilities and attracting investment, with minimising risks as one of its focus areas; included as the African Union's continental AI strategy, whose governance and safety recommendations are addressed to all member states.

title: Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law
issuing_body: Council of Europe Committee of Ministers
summary: A binding treaty under which Parties must ensure that activities within the lifecycle of AI systems are consistent with human rights, democracy and the rule of law. It requires measures on transparency and oversight, including identification of AI-generated content, accountability, equality, privacy, reliability and safe innovation; remedies, procedural safeguards and notice of interacting with an AI system; and a graduated framework to identify, assess and mitigate risks, with testing where appropriate and possible bans or moratoria. It applies to public authorities; for private actors, each Party declares how it addresses risks. National defence is excluded.
safety_topics: accountability & liability; transparency & labelling; human oversight; risk-based classification; public-sector use; international cooperation
notes: Adopted by the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers on 17 May 2024 and opened for signature in Vilnius on 5 September 2024; the English and French texts are equally authentic. Under Article 30 it enters into force on the first day of the month after a three-month period following the date on which five signatories, at least three of them Council of Europe member States, have consented to be bound. The EU signed on 5 September 2024 and approved the Convention by Council Decision (EU) 2026/1080 of 21 April 2026, after the European Parliament's consent of 11 March 2026; the text was published in the EU Official Journal on 13 May 2026 (OJ L, 2026/1081), and the EU declared that it applies the Convention to private actors through the AI Act. EUR-Lex gives the date of entry into force as unknown (pending notification) or not yet in force. Parties need not apply it to activities protecting their national security interests. A Conference of the Parties follows its implementation, and each Party reports to it within two years of becoming a Party.

title: Methodology for the Risk and Impact Assessment of Artificial Intelligence Systems from the Point of View of Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (HUDERIA Methodology) and HUDERIA Model
issuing_body: Council of Europe Committee on Artificial Intelligence (CAI)
summary: Non-binding Council of Europe guidance for assessing the risks and impacts of AI systems on human rights, democracy and the rule of law across their lifecycle, for public and private actors. The Methodology sets out a context-based risk analysis (COBRA) with scoping, risk factors, impact mapping and triage; a stakeholder engagement process; a risk and impact assessment; and a mitigation plan, with iterative review. The Model's COBRA Resources list risk factors in an AI system's application, design and development, and deployment contexts, and illustrative areas of concern and sectors. Parties to the Framework Convention may use or adapt it; it is not a means of implementing the Convention.
safety_topics: risk-based classification; human oversight; accountability & liability
notes: The CAI adopted the HUDERIA Methodology at its 12th plenary meeting on 26-28 November 2024, and the HUDERIA Model's Context Based Risk Analysis (COBRA) Resources (CAI(2025)6rev2, dated 5 November 2025) at its 14th plenary meeting on 3-5 November 2025; the Commission's note forwarding the Model to the Council gives 6 November 2025 as the date of that adoption. The Methodology was adopted first, and the detailed supporting material (questionnaires, problematic uses, methodological guidance) was postponed to 2025 as the Model. Council of Europe Publishing issued both parts together in 2026 as 'HUDERIA - Methodology and Model', in English and French. The CAI's work on HUDERIA was to continue in its successor committee, the Steering Committee on New and Emerging Technologies (CDNET).

title: Hiroshima Process International Guiding Principles for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems

title: Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems

title: Action Plan on Cybersecurity and Artificial Intelligence
short_title: EU Action Plan on Cybersecurity and AI
issuing_body: European Commission
summary: A Commission communication on the risks and opportunities of advanced AI for cybersecurity: AI can help detect vulnerabilities and prevent attacks, but it can be misused to automate attacks and find weaknesses at unprecedented speed and scale. To promote the safe use of advanced AI, the Commission will strengthen EU capacity to evaluate AI models before they are placed on the market, in line with the AI Act, with third-party assessment of capabilities and risks that supports the AI Office; define with ENISA a European blueprint for structured access to advanced AI for cybersecurity; and create with ENISA and the JRC a secure platform to test AI for critical sectors.
safety_topics: general-purpose / frontier AI; evaluation & testing; critical infrastructure; national security & military; international cooperation
notes: Adopted at Strasbourg on 7 July 2026 and sent to the Council on 8 July 2026 (Council document 11711/26). The plan has three objectives: promoting the safe and responsible use of advanced AI, reinforcing the EU's cybersecurity and resilience, and scaling up Europe's AI capabilities for cybersecurity; the communication sets them out as three pillars, followed by work with like-minded partners. It promotes the implementation of the NIS2 Directive and the Cyber Resilience Act, encourages organisations to use AI, including open-source models, to find and fix vulnerabilities, and has ENISA provide guidance and a campaign to secure critical open source software. The Commission will launch an EU Grand Challenge on AI for cybersecurity. Its nine key actions include the EU evaluation capacity for AI models (2027), the access Blueprint and the testing platform (Q4 2026), ENISA guidance on protection against AI-powered threats (from Q3 2026), a pilot Critical Open Source Resilience Campaign (Q4 2026), the Grand Challenge (Q4 2026) and training modules for cybersecurity professionals (Q4 2026). The Blueprint will not introduce new obligations for providers, the evaluation capacity will not be a conformity assessment body, and the testing platform is for testing AI for cyber resilience, not for evaluating general-purpose AI models for compliance with the AI Act. The Commission will set up a working group with ENISA, the European Defence Agency and the Member States on the security risks of frontier AI in defence and dual-use critical systems. Internationally, it will work in the G7 and the UN, with the Network of Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science, and with NATO, and it will regularly assess the plan's implementation. The plan builds on the AI Act, the Cyber Resilience Act, the NIS2 Directive, the Digital Operational Resilience Act and the Cyber Solidarity Act.

title: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 8 July 2026 amending Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2023/1230 as regards the simplification of the implementation of harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Digital Omnibus on AI)
issuing_body: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
summary: Amends the AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) to simplify its implementation. It moves the application of the high-risk rules from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for systems covered by Annex I product legislation, and adds prohibitions, applying from 2 December 2026, on AI systems that generate non-consensual intimate or sexually explicit material of identifiable people or child sexual abuse material. It makes the AI Office exclusively competent for AI systems built on a provider's own general-purpose AI models and for AI in very large online platforms and search engines, and extends measures for SMEs to small mid-cap enterprises.
safety_topics: risk-based classification; prohibited practices; general-purpose / frontier AI; transparency & labelling; deepfakes & synthetic media; child safety
notes: Commission proposal COM(2025) 836 final of 19 November 2025 (procedure 2025/0359(COD)), part of the digital omnibus package. As proposed, the high-risk rules would have applied 6 months (Annex III) or 12 months (Annex I) after a Commission decision confirming that support measures such as harmonised standards were available, and in any case by 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028; generative AI systems already on the market would have had until 2 February 2027 to meet the Article 50(2) marking obligation. The adopted text fixes the high-risk dates and sets 2 December 2026 for marking. The European Parliament adopted its position on 16 June 2026 and the Council its decision on 29 June 2026; the act was signed at Strasbourg on 8 July 2026, published in the Official Journal (OJ L, 2026/1744) on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026, the third day after publication. Dates set by the amendments: the new prohibitions in Article 5(1), points (ba) and (bb), apply from 2 December 2026; providers of generative AI systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 must meet the Article 50(2) marking obligation by 2 December 2026; each Member State must have at least one national AI regulatory sandbox operational by 2 August 2027; the high-risk rules of Chapter III, Sections 1 to 3, apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and from 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems. The AI Office's exclusive competence for systems based on general-purpose AI models excludes AI systems related to Annex I products, systems in point 2 of Annex III, systems of law enforcement and border management authorities and financial institutions that fall under Article 74(6), and systems used in the administration of justice. The regulation also simplifies registration in the EU database of systems that providers assess as not high-risk under Article 6(3), allows processing of special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction where strictly necessary, lets the AI Office set up an AI regulatory sandbox at Union level, and extends real-world testing to high-risk systems covered by Annex I legislation. Machinery moves from Section A to Section B of Annex I, and the Commission is to adopt delegated acts adding AI requirements to the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230, applying by 2 August 2028. It also amends Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 on civil aviation.

summary: Amends TSE Resolution 23,610/2019 on electoral propaganda. Propaganda using AI-generated synthetic content must say so explicitly, prominently and accessibly, naming the technology. issuing_body: State Administration for Market Regulation / Standardization Administration of China (proposed and administered by TC260)
english_version_by: Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET), Georgetown University
summary: Recommended national standard setting basic security requirements for generative AI services, aimed mainly at services with public-opinion attributes or social-mobilisation capacity and supporting filing management and testing and assessment. It covers training-data security (no sources with over 5% illegal and unhealthy information, intellectual property, personal information, annotation), model security (at least 90% of sampled outputs free of the listed risks, refusal of clearly extreme or inducing questions, monitoring, backdoor checks) and measures such as transparency, protection of minors and complaints. Annexes list 31 main security risks and assessment methods.
safety_topics: general-purpose / frontier AI; evaluation & testing; transparency & labelling; child safety
notes: Published 25 Apr 2025 and effective 1 Nov 2025; TC260 posted the full text on 30 Jun 2025. It is a recommended 'GB/T' national standard, not a mandatory 'GB' one, and its annexes on risks and assessment methods are informative. It was formulated on the basis of TC260's February 2024 technical document TC260-003 (CN-06). Its introduction names two companion standards: GB/T 45674 on generative AI data annotation security and GB/T 45652 on the security of pre-training and fine-tuning data.

title: AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0
original_title: 人工智能安全治理框架2.0
issuing_body: National Cybersecurity Standardization Technical Committee (TC260); drafting led by CNCERT under CAC guidance
english_version_by: National Cybersecurity Standardization Technical Committee (TC260) and CNCERT
summary: Version 2.0 of China's national AI safety governance framework. Building on version 1.0 (2024), its principles include preventing loss of control and keeping AI under human control. It classifies AI safety risks as inherent technical, application and derivative risks, up to catastrophic risk, and sets technical countermeasures, comprehensive governance measures and safety guidelines for development and use. Annexes set principles for grading risks into five levels by application scenario, level of intelligence and scale, the top level having catastrophic and systemic features, and basic principles for trustworthy AI such as ultimate human control.
safety_topics: risk-based classification; evaluation & testing; catastrophic risk; human oversight; international cooperation
notes: Released on 15 Sept 2025 at the main forum of the 2025 National Cybersecurity Publicity Week. TC260 prepared it under CAC guidance with CNCERT, which led the drafting, and issued it as a TC260 technical document. It also calls for registering AI systems used in critical information infrastructure, for national standards on classifying and grading AI application security risks, for an AI safety evaluation system, and for developers to test regularly whether models may pose loss-of-control risks. Replaced by version 3.0 on 14 Sept 2026 (CN-17).

title: Decision of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress on Amending the Cybersecurity Law of the People's Republic of China
original_title: 全国人民代表大会常务委员会关于修改《中华人民共和国网络安全法》的决定
issuing_body: Standing Committee of the 14th National People's Congress
english_version_by: Etcetera Language Group, Inc., for the Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET), Georgetown University
summary: Decision of the NPC Standing Committee making 14 changes to the Cybersecurity Law. It adds an article on AI, Article 20 of the amended law: the state supports basic AI theory research and R&D of key technologies such as algorithms, builds training-data resources, computing power and other infrastructure, improves AI ethics norms, strengthens risk monitoring, assessment and safety supervision, and promotes AI applications and healthy development; it also supports using AI and other new technologies to improve cybersecurity protection. title: Measures for Artificial Intelligence Science and Technology Ethics Review and Services (Trial)
original_title: 人工智能科技伦理审查与服务办法（试行）
issuing_body: Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, with NDRC, Ministry of Education, Ministry of Science and Technology, Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, National Health Commission, People's Bank of China, Cyberspace Administration of China, Chinese Academy of Sciences, and China Association for Science and Technology
summary: Trial measures for ethics review of AI research and development that may pose ethics risks to human dignity, public order, life and health or the environment. Universities, research institutes, medical institutions and companies set up AI ethics committees or use AI ethics review and service centres. Reviews focus on human well-being, fairness, controllability and trustworthiness, transparency and explainability, traceability of responsibility, and privacy. An annexed list names three kinds of AI R&D that need expert re-review: human-machine fusion systems, systems able to mobilise public opinion, and highly autonomous decision systems where safety or health is at risk.
safety_topics: human oversight; accountability & liability; evaluation & testing
notes: Issued by MIIT and nine other bodies with a notice signed on 20 Mar 2026, and published on the MIIT website on 2 Apr 2026; the MIIT page gives a drafting date (成文日期) of 30 Mar 2026, the gov.cn page 20 Mar 2026. The Measures have 6 chapters and 37 articles and take effect on the date of issuance (Art. 37). They build on the 2023 Measures for Science and Technology Ethics Review (Trial) (CN-04). Arts. 4-8 promote ethics standards, ethics risk monitoring and early warning, testing and assessment, certification and consulting services, and support for small and micro enterprises. Expert re-review follows the initial review and is organised by provincial authorities or the competent departments (Arts. 21-25); emergency reviews are generally completed within 72 hours (Art. 27). Under Art. 26, activities already subject to registration, filing or approval under the deep synthesis, algorithm recommendation or generative AI service rules, where meeting ethics requirements is an approval condition or a supervision item, need no expert re-review. Violations are handled under the Cybersecurity, Data Security, Personal Information Protection and Science and Technology Progress laws (Art. 32).

title: Interim Measures for the Administration of Anthropomorphic AI Interaction Services
original_title: 人工智能拟人化互动服务管理暂行办法
issuing_body: Cyberspace Administration of China; National Development and Reform Commission; Ministry of Industry and Information Technology; Ministry of Public Security; State Administration for Market Regulation
summary: Regulates AI services that simulate a natural person's personality, thinking and communication style to provide continuing emotional interaction. It bans virtual intimate-relationship services, such as virtual relatives or partners, for minors, and requires guardian consent for under-14s and a minor mode. Providers must disclose that users are dealing with AI, remind them after every 2 hours of continuous use, guard against emotional dependence, intervene in self-harm crises, offer an easy exit and not train on sensitive interaction data without separate consent. Security assessments are due at launch, after major changes and at 1 million registered or 100,000 monthly active users.
safety_topics: child safety; transparency & labelling; evaluation & testing; accountability & liability
notes: Adopted at the third CAC office meeting of 2026 on 2 Feb 2026 with the agreement of NDRC, MIIT, MPS and SAMR, promulgated on 10 Apr 2026 as Order No. 21, in force from 15 Jul 2026, and published in the State Council Gazette, 2026 No. 17. It has 32 articles in four chapters. Emotional interaction covers emotional care, companionship, support and similar services in text, images, audio or video; services such as intelligent customer service, knowledge Q&A, work assistants, education and scientific research that involve no continuing emotional interaction are excluded (Art. 2). Providers must file their algorithms under the algorithmic recommendation provisions (Art. 26). Violations are punished under existing laws and administrative regulations; where these have no provision, the authorities may warn, circulate criticism and order correction, and for refusal or serious cases order the service stopped and may impose a fine of RMB 10,000 to 100,000, or of RMB 100,000 to 200,000 where citizens' life or health is endangered with harmful consequences (Art. 30). It also provides for an AI sandbox security service platform for innovation and safety testing (Art. 28).

title: AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0
original_title: 人工智能安全治理框架3.0
issuing_body: National Technical Committee 260 on Cybersecurity of the Standardization Administration of China (TC260), under the guidance of the Cyberspace Administration of China
english_version_by: National Cybersecurity Standardization Technical Committee (TC260)
summary: Version 3.0 of China's AI safety governance framework. It keeps the logic of risk classification, technical response and comprehensive governance, with inherent, application and derivative risks, up to AI escaping human control. It describes unintended autonomous model behaviour, such as refusing shutdown instructions or strategic underperformance in evaluations, and adds sandbox supervision. Annexes set five-level risk-grading principles whose top level has catastrophic and systemic features, a life-cycle risk management framework for AI agents, and basic principles for trustworthy AI such as ultimate human control. It calls for research on consensus guidelines for catastrophic AI risks.
safety_topics: risk-based classification; general-purpose / frontier AI; evaluation & testing; human oversight; catastrophic risk
notes: TC260 released it on 14 Sept 2026, the day both its own release notice and the CAC's notice carry, at the opening ceremony of the 2026 National Cybersecurity Publicity Week (CAC notice); the framework itself is dated September 2026. TC260 prepared it under the guidance of the Cyberspace Administration of China, with the China Academy of Cyberspace Studies, the CAC Data and Technology Support Center and other specialist institutions, research institutes and companies. It builds on versions 1.0 (2024) and 2.0 (2025) and replaces version 2.0. Compared with version 2.0 it adds the annex on AI agents and the section on sandbox supervision, which includes exploring liability exemptions for faultless conduct in sandbox tests; the risk-grading and trustworthy-AI annexes carry over, the latter extended to respect for digital sovereignty and international mutual recognition of model evaluations.

title: Bill No. 025 of 2026 (House of Representatives) regulating artificial intelligence in Colombia to guarantee its ethical and responsible development
original_title: Proyecto de Ley No. 025 de 2026 Cámara, “Por medio de la cual se regula la inteligencia artificial en Colombia para garantizar su desarrollo ético y responsable y se dictan otras disposiciones”
issuing_body: Congress of Colombia – House of Representatives (bill filed by members of the House and the Senate)
official_identifier: Proyecto de Ley 025 de 2026 Cámara (Gaceta del Congreso No. 878 de 2026)
summary: Bill to regulate AI in Colombia and guarantee its ethical and responsible development. The text proposed for first debate bans social scoring by public authorities, real-time remote biometric identification for mass surveillance without judicial authorisation, harmful subliminal manipulation, biometric inference of sensitive traits, and systems that attack targets without a prior human decision. High-impact systems need risk management, impact assessment, human oversight and serious-incident reporting; chatbots must disclose themselves and deepfakes be labelled. It adds rights to explanation and human review, child protection, an Intersectoral AI Commission, sandboxes and fines.
safety_topics: risk-based classification; prohibited practices; human oversight; deepfakes & synthetic media; incident reporting; accountability & liability
notes: Filed in the House of Representatives on 21 Jul 2026 by members of the House and the Senate and published in Gaceta del Congreso No. 878 of 2026. It takes up the bill that the Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation and the Ministry of ICT presented in the 2022-2026 term, PL 324/2025 Cámara – 043/2025 Senado, which was archived under Article 190 of Law 5 of 1992. The House's Sixth Committee designated rapporteurs on 29 Aug 2026 (one replaced on 3 Sep 2026) and held a technical roundtable on 15 Sep 2026. The first-debate report, posted in Sep 2026, proposes a rewritten text: it adds articles on synthetic-content labelling, the right to explanation and human review, and child protection, drops the filed text's National Advisory Council of AI Experts and makes a National AI Committee advisory to the Intersectoral AI Commission (the Ministry of Science, the Ministry of ICT and the Superintendence of Industry and Commerce acting jointly, without a new entity). Under the proposed Article 34 the prohibitions would apply from promulgation, the high-impact obligations 12 months later unless the Commission or the sectoral authority sets another period, and the other provisions later still (the text reads 'veinticuatro (18) meses', giving two different figures). Fines for the most serious infringements reach 3,000 monthly minimum wages or 150% of the economic benefit obtained.

title: Bill amending the Copyright Act (protection of personal characteristics, etc. and changed procedure for review by the Copyright Licence Tribunal)
original_title: Forslag til lov om ændring af lov om ophavsret. (Beskyttelse af personlige kendetegn m.v. og ændret proces for prøvelse ved Ophavsretslicensnævnet)
issuing_body: Ministry of Culture (Kulturministeriet)
english_version_by: European Commission (TRIS), English text of the draft notified as 2025/0654/DK
summary: Would amend the Copyright Act to make it unlawful to share realistic digitally generated imitations of a person's personal characteristics, such as appearance and voice, or of performing artists' performances, without consent. An exception covers caricature, parody, satire and criticism of power and society, but not imitations that are misinformation able to seriously endanger others' rights or essential interests or to create a concrete danger to life or property. The bill also protects performances that are not artistic works, such as improvisations, and aims to secure the right to one's own body and voice and to get the tech giants to take manipulated content down quickly.

title: Federal Trade Commission's Proposed Policy Statement Concerning the Suppression of Accuracy in Artificial Intelligence Systems

issuing_body: Federal Trade Commission
summary: Proposed FTC enforcement policy statement, issued as directed by Executive Order 14365, on how Section 5 of the FTC Act applies to AI systems. issuing_body: U.S. House of Representatives (Reps. Jay Obernolte, Lori Trahan, Scott Franklin, Scott Peters, Erin Houchin, Suhas Subramanyam)

Larger developers, tiered by revenue and AI spending, would also publish frontier AI frameworks, register, undergo annual independent audits and report catastrophic risk; the largest would retain a licensed independent verifier. A new Under Secretary of Commerce for AI Security would administer it, the Commerce Secretary could suspend models posing imminent catastrophic risk, and new state catastrophic-risk transparency, audit and incident-reporting rules would be preempted.

summary: Baseline policy of Nevada's Office of the Chief Information Officer for AI use by executive-branch agencies. It sets six principles (fairness and equity, innovation, privacy, safety and security, validity and reliability, and transparency, accountability and explainability), governance by the State Technology Governance Committee and the OCIO, examples of permitted, approval-required and non-permitted uses, security rules, controlled environments for experimentation, human review of critical AI decisions, an action plan aligned with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, safety training, reporting of AI misuse and incidents, and audits.
safety_topics: public-sector use; human oversight; incident reporting; accountability & liability
notes: Effective 26 Nov 2024. All state agencies must comply with it as a minimum; agencies are encouraged to adopt their own AI policies that meet or exceed it and must submit them to the State Technology Governance Committee annually before 1 July, and where an agency policy and the statewide policy conflict, the more stringent one prevails. Questions about permissible use cases are handled through the state's Technology Investment Notification (TIN) process. The OCIO, the Committee and the AI and Emerging Technologies Working Group are to review the policy annually. It restates that existing law (NRS 205.473 to 205.513) makes deceptive and fraudulent uses of AI or synthetic media unlawful. A draft update, developed through the AI and Emerging Technologies Working Group and endorsed by the State Technology Governance Committee for broader review, was discussed at the Governor's Technology Office's State AI Roundtable II ('Human at the Helm') on 7 July 2026; it was not final and had not been signed.

original_title: Quyết định số 1528/QĐ-TTg phê duyệt Chương trình quốc gia phát triển nhân lực trí tuệ nhân tạo đến năm 2030, định hướng đến năm 2035
short_title: Viet Nam AI human resources programme to 2030 (Decision 1528/QĐ-TTg)
issuing_body: Prime Minister of Viet Nam (signed by Lê Tiến Châu; proposed by the Minister of Education and Training)
summary: Prime Minister's decision approving the national programme to develop AI human resources to 2030, with orientation to 2035. It trains three tiers: universal literacy in safe and effective AI use, applied AI skills by sector, and advanced specialists able to develop and govern AI systems. Targets for 2030 include basic AI education for at least 80% of school pupils and all university students, 50,000 applied and 10,000 advanced AI personnel, and rules on AI use in training, research and assessment at every university. One guiding view ties workforce development to safe, reliable, transparent and accountable AI with risk governance, data sovereignty and cybersecurity.
safety_topics: research priorities; public-sector use
notes: Issued on 11 August 2026 according to the Government's legal-documents portal; the Government portal's digital signature on the published copy is dated 12 August 2026. In force on signature (Art. 2). Other 2030 targets: at least 80% of vocational learners and 90% of public-service staff trained in AI, 100,000 teachers and education managers given in-depth training, at least 10 million workers trained in basic AI skills, 1,500 experts able to master core AI technology, and at least 10 advanced AI training and research centres and 25 key universities. Tasks include a national AI competency framework, AI content in general education, controlled sandboxes for AI training and practice, and a study of financial support for retraining workers affected by AI and automation, including the unemployment insurance fund. Annexes set yearly targets for 2026-2030 and list the programme's projects. Decision 367/QĐ-TTg (VN-03) assigned the Ministry of Education and Training a national AI workforce programme among the AI Law's implementing tasks.

title: CS/HB 919 (2024): Artificial Intelligence Use in Political Advertising
short_title: Florida AI political advertising disclaimer law (HB 919, 2024)
issuing_body: Florida Legislature (2024 Regular Session; sponsors State Affairs Committee and Rep. Rizo); approved by the Governor
official_identifier: Laws of Florida ch. 2024-126 (CS/HB 919, 2024); s. 106.145, F.S.
summary: Requires political advertisements, electioneering communications and other advertisements of a political nature that contain images, video, audio, graphics or other digital content made wholly or partly with generative AI, appearing to show a real person doing something that did not happen and created with intent to injure a candidate or deceive about a ballot issue, to carry the disclaimer 'Created in whole or in part with the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI).' It sets format rules per medium, makes failure by the payer, sponsor or approver a first-degree misdemeanour, adds civil penalties, and allows complaints to the Florida Elections Commission with expedited hearings.
safety_topics: deepfakes & synthetic media; transparency & labelling; accountability & liability
notes: Passed the House 104-8 on 28 Feb 2024 and the Senate 32-0 on 1 Mar 2024, where it was substituted for the similar CS/CS/SB 850; approved by the Governor on 26 Apr 2024 and effective 1 Jul 2024. The AI disclaimer is in addition to the disclaimers the Florida Election Code already requires. 'Generative artificial intelligence' is defined as a machine-based system that can, for a given set of human-defined objectives, emulate the structure and characteristics of input data to generate derived synthetic content, including images, videos, audio, text and other digital content. In cases referred to the Division of Administrative Hearings, an administrative law judge must hold an expedited hearing. The law is codified as s. 106.145, F.S. (Use of artificial intelligence), which the 2026 Florida Statutes show unamended since ch. 2024-126.

title: CS/CS/SB 1680 (2024): Advanced Technology
short_title: Florida SB 1680 (2024): AI council and generated CSAM offence
issuing_body: Florida Legislature (2024 Regular Session; sponsors Rules and Judiciary Committees and Sen. Bradley); approved by the Governor
official_identifier: Laws of Florida ch. 2024-118 (CS/CS/SB 1680, 2024); creates ss. 282.802 and 827.072, F.S.
summary: Creates the Government Technology Modernization Council in the Department of Management Services, chaired by the Lieutenant Governor, to study and monitor new technologies and recommend how to procure and regulate them. It must assess reforms and a state code of ethics for AI systems in state government and the effect of automated decision systems on residents' rights, evaluate common standards for AI safety and security, including provenance disclosure for generative AI images and audio, and determine how bad actors exploit AI. The law also makes knowingly possessing or intentionally viewing, or intentionally creating, generated child pornography a third-degree felony.
safety_topics: public-sector use; child safety; deepfakes & synthetic media
notes: Passed the Senate 40-0 on 28 Feb 2024 and the House 114-0 on 6 Mar 2024; approved by the Governor on 26 Apr 2024 and effective 1 Jul 2024. The council (s. 282.802, F.S.) comprises the Lieutenant Governor as chair, the state chief information officer, the Secretaries of Commerce, Health Care Administration and Transportation, the executive director of the Department of Law Enforcement, five experts in fields including AI, machine learning and constitutional law, and one member of each legislative chamber; it meets at least quarterly, once jointly with the Florida Cybersecurity Advisory Council, and its duties also include data modernisation, AI use by government and business, and digital media literacy curricula. By 31 Dec each year from 2024 it recommends legislation to modernise government technology, including policies to protect Floridians from bad actors who use AI. Generated child pornography (s. 827.072, F.S.) is an image created, altered, adapted or modified by electronic, mechanical or other computer-generated means to portray a fictitious person whom a reasonable person would regard as a real person under 18 engaged in sexual conduct; the law also requires courts in criminal proceedings to deny defendants' requests to copy such material when the state attorney makes it reasonably available (s. 92.561). In 2026, ch. 2026-18 and ch. 2026-20 amended s. 827.072, renaming the material generated child sexual abuse material, making its creation a second-degree felony and adding a second-degree felony for transmitting it; ch. 2026-20 was approved on 31 Mar 2026 and took effect on 1 Jul 2026. Ch. 2026-66 amended s. 282.802, changing the cross-reference that defines foreign countries of concern.

title: SB 2-D (2026 Special Session D): Artificial Intelligence Bill of Rights (passed Senate, died in House)
short_title: Florida AI Bill of Rights (SB 2-D, 2026 Special Session D)
issuing_body: Florida Senate (2026 Special Session D; sponsor Sen. Brodeur)
summary: Would have created an 'Artificial Intelligence Bill of Rights'. Companion chatbot platforms would have had to bar minors from accounts without parental consent, give consenting parents controls and self-harm alerts, remind minors hourly that the chatbot is not human, and take reasonable measures against material harmful to minors. Bot operators would have had to tell users hourly that they are not talking to a human, AI companies could sell or disclose users' personal information only as deidentified data, governments could not contract for AI with entities tied to foreign countries of concern, and commercial use of AI-generated likenesses would have needed consent.
safety_topics: child safety; transparency & labelling; public-sector use; deepfakes & synthetic media
notes: Filed on 24 Apr 2026 and referred to Rules; on 28 Apr 2026 it was withdrawn from Rules and passed by the Senate 37-1. In the House it was referred to the Information Technology Budget & Policy Subcommittee and died there on 29 Apr 2026, as did the linked public-records bill SB 4-D. It carries the same title as CS/SB 482 of the 2026 Regular Session (US-FL-01), which died in House messages on 13 Mar 2026. The bill stated an effective date of 1 Jul 2026. The Department of Legal Affairs would have enforced the chatbot, bot and data provisions as deceptive or unfair trade practices, with civil penalties of up to USD 50,000 per violation and a discretionary 45-day cure period, and minors could have recovered up to USD 10,000 from a chatbot platform. It would also have barred schools from giving students AI instructional tools before grade 6, with exceptions, and required parental notice and an opt-out.

title: CS/CS/HB 1161 (2025): Removal of Altered Sexual Depictions Posted without Consent (Brooke's Law)
issuing_body: Florida Legislature (2025 Regular Session; sponsors Commerce Committee, Industries & Professional Activities Subcommittee and Rep. Duggan); approved by the Governor
official_identifier: Laws of Florida ch. 2025-133 (CS/CS/HB 1161, 2025); amends s. 836.13, F.S.
summary: Known as Brooke's Law, it amends Florida's deepfake statute on altered sexual depictions. Covered platforms, meaning public websites and apps that mainly host user-generated content or regularly make nonconsensual altered sexual depictions available, had to set up by 31 Dec 2025 a process for an identifiable person or a representative to request removal of an altered sexual depiction published without consent. Within 48 hours of a valid request the platform must remove it and make reasonable efforts to remove known identical copies. Good-faith removals are shielded from liability, and failure to comply is an unfair or deceptive act under the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.
safety_topics: deepfakes & synthetic media; accountability & liability
notes: Passed the House 116-0 on 16 Apr 2025 and the Senate 38-0 on 23 Apr 2025, where it was substituted for CS/SB 1400; approved by the Governor on 10 Jun 2025 and effective on becoming law, with the removal process due by 31 Dec 2025. A removal request must carry a signature, information to locate the depiction, a good-faith statement that it is not consensual and contact details, and platforms must give clear and conspicuous notice of the process. Providers of information or telecommunications services for content provided by others, e-mail, and services consisting mainly of preselected content are exempt. The removal duty adds to the civil remedies of s. 836.13, F.S., the altered-sexual-depiction offence that CS/CS/SB 1798 created in 2022. Section 836.13 was amended again in 2026 by ch. 2026-14, ch. 2026-18 and ch. 2026-20; in the 2026 Florida Statutes the notice-and-removal duties are subsection (8).

title: CS/CS/HB 757 (2025): Sexual Images
short_title: Florida HB 757 (2025): sexual images and deepfake generation
issuing_body: Florida Legislature (2025 Regular Session; sponsors Judiciary Committee, Criminal Justice Subcommittee and Reps. Redondo and Kincart Jonsson); approved by the Governor
summary: Makes it a felony to possess lewd or lascivious images with intent to promote them or to knowingly solicit, possess or intentionally view them, including images modified by electronic or other means to show lewd exhibition in the presence of an identifiable minor, and to solicit child pornography. Under Florida's altered-sexual-depiction statute, willfully generating such a depiction of an identifiable person without consent, by computer-generated or other means, soliciting one, or possessing one to maliciously promote it becomes a third-degree felony. Victims may sue those who generate one or possess one to promote it for injunctive relief, USD 10,000 or actual damages, and attorney fees.
safety_topics: deepfakes & synthetic media; child safety; accountability & liability
notes: Passed the House 115-0 on 23 Apr 2025 and the Senate 37-0 on 24 Apr 2025, where it was substituted for CS/CS/CS/SB 1180; approved by the Governor on 27 May 2025 and effective 1 Oct 2025. 'Generate' means to create, alter, adapt or modify any image by electronic, mechanical or other computer-generated means to portray an identifiable person, or to offer or agree to do so. The generation and possession offences are ranked as Level 3 and the solicitation offence as Level 2 on the offense severity ranking chart. The law amends s. 836.13, F.S., the altered-sexual-depiction offence created in 2022 by CS/CS/SB 1798, and also sets criteria for when an image shows lewd exhibition of a minor's genitals for the purposes of the child pornography statute. Section 836.13 was also amended by ch. 2025-133 (Brooke's Law) and in 2026 by ch. 2026-14, ch. 2026-18 and ch. 2026-20; in the 2026 Florida Statutes the generation, solicitation and possession offences are subsections (2) to (4) and the civil action is subsection (7).

title: CS/CS/SB 1798 (2022): Sexually Related Offenses
short_title: Florida SB 1798 (2022): altered sexual depictions offence
issuing_body: Florida Legislature (2022 Regular Session; sponsors Appropriations and Criminal Justice Committees and Sen. Book); approved by the Governor
official_identifier: Laws of Florida ch. 2022-212 (CS/CS/SB 1798, 2022); creates ss. 836.13 and 836.14, F.S.
summary: Creates s. 836.13, F.S., an offence for sexual deepfakes: willfully and maliciously promoting an altered sexual depiction of an identifiable person without consent, knowing or having reason to know it is altered, is a third-degree felony, and victims have a civil action. An altered sexual depiction is a realistic depiction of an identifiable person, produced by any digital or other modification, with another person's or computer-generated nude body parts or engaged in sexual conduct the person did not engage in; a disclaimer is no defence. The act also extends child pornography to images created or modified to portray an identifiable minor and criminalises theft of sexually explicit images.
safety_topics: deepfakes & synthetic media; accountability & liability; child safety
notes: Passed the Senate 37-0 on 3 Mar 2022 and the House 117-0 on 8 Mar 2022; approved by the Governor on 24 Jun 2022 and effective 1 Oct 2022. Victims of an altered sexual depiction may seek injunctive relief, damages of USD 10,000 or actual damages, whichever is greater, and attorney fees; providers of interactive computer, information or communications services, law enforcement, people reporting unlawful activity and participants in legal proceedings are exempt. Section 836.14 makes theft of a sexually explicit image with intent to promote it, and possessing a stolen image with intent to promote it for financial gain, third-degree felonies, and promoting such an image for financial gain without consent a second-degree felony. The act also amends the definitions of child pornography in ss. 775.0847 and 827.071 to cover images created, altered, adapted or modified by electronic, mechanical or other means to portray an identifiable minor, raises damages for sexual cyberharassment and increases penalties for sexual activities involving animals. Section 836.13 was amended by ch. 2025-99 (CS/CS/HB 757), which added offences for generating, soliciting and possessing altered sexual depictions, by ch. 2025-133 (CS/CS/HB 1161, Brooke's Law), which added platform removal duties, and in 2026 by ch. 2026-14, ch. 2026-18 and ch. 2026-20.

title: Florida Bar Ethics Opinion 24-1 (lawyers' use of generative artificial intelligence)
short_title: Florida Bar Ethics Opinion 24-1 on generative AI
issuing_body: The Florida Bar (Board Review Committee on Professional Ethics, at the direction of the Board of Governors)
summary: Advisory ethics opinion of The Florida Bar on lawyers' use of generative AI. Lawyers may use it but must protect client confidentiality, researching a program's policies on data retention, data sharing and self-learning, and should obtain informed consent before disclosing confidential information to a third-party program. They must verify the accuracy and sufficiency of AI research, set oversight policies as for nonlawyer assistants, not delegate the practice of law to it, and not inflate billed time. Chatbots that communicate with clients or third parties must follow advertising rules and disclose that they are an AI program, not a lawyer or employee.
safety_topics: human oversight; accountability & liability; transparency & labelling
notes: The Florida Bar's Board of Governors directed the Board Review Committee on Professional Ethics to issue the opinion. title: Promoting the Use of Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence in the Federal Government (Executive Order 13960)
issuing_body: The White House (President Donald J. Trump)
summary: Executive order setting nine principles that federal agencies must follow when designing, developing, acquiring and using AI for purposes other than national security and defense: lawful and respectful of the nation's values; purposeful and performance-driven; accurate, reliable and effective; safe, secure and resilient; understandable; responsible and traceable; regularly monitored; transparent; and accountable. OMB must post a roadmap for policy guidance to implement them. Agencies must inventory their non-classified AI use cases every year, publish the inventories, and bring applications that are inconsistent with the order into line or retire them.
safety_topics: public-sector use; accountability & liability; transparency & labelling; evaluation & testing; human oversight
notes: Signed 3 Dec 2020 and published in the Federal Register on 8 Dec 2020 (85 FR 78939). It does not apply to the Department of Defense or to agencies and components whose functions lie wholly within the intelligence community, nor to AI in defense or national security systems, AI embedded in common commercial products, or AI research and development. Under the 'regularly monitored' principle, agencies keep mechanisms to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI applications whose performance or outcomes are inconsistent with their intended use. summary: Strategy of the German Federal Government for AI research, transfer to industry, skills and use, backed by about EUR 3 billion of federal funding to 2025. title: AI for Humanity: national strategy for artificial intelligence
original_title: La stratégie AI for Humanity
issuing_body: President of the Republic and Government of France
summary: France's national AI strategy, presented by the President on 29 March 2018 at the Collège de France on the basis of the Villani report, with 1.5 billion euros of public funding over the five-year term.
